solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Bishop and I will advertise a list of actors

definitions.note: a noun phrase; the answer works as both verb and noun

blocks.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
the contraction I'll, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A churchman and a performer plan to put up a poster naming the cast.
explanation.walkthrough: B and I'LL make BILL, which here does double duty: to bill a show is to advertise it, and the bill is the printed list of performers.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatres post bills to promote shows, and the bill also names who is appearing, as in top of the bill.

clue.text: Bank on the Bard’s flying cloud and first of some ironic cheers

indicators.note: asking for the first of something keeps only its opening letter

blocks.note: a bar is a sandbank across a river mouth
Shakespeare uses rack for driven, wind-blown cloud
the opening letter of 'some'

explanation.surface: Someone stakes everything on a Shakespearean cloud while the crowd offers sarcastic applause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank on' looks like a phrase meaning rely on, but 'Bank' alone is the sandbank and 'on' just stacks it above the next piece in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To barrack is to jeer or heckle a performer, so cheering ironically at someone is exactly that mockery.

clue.text: McGonagall’s sort of grey lyric, free of accepted craft

indicators.note: being free of something means it has been taken away, so a letter goes

blocks.note: a lay is a song or short lyric poem
A is the abbreviation for accepted, as marked on bills of exchange
craft in the sense of skill or artistry

explanation.surface: A note on the dull, grey verse of a famously bad poet, which lacks any recognised skill.
explanation.walkthrough: William McGonagall was a Scottish poet notorious as the worst in English, so his name flags a Scots word. 'Lyric' is a noun here, the song LAY, losing its A.
explanation.definitionFit: Lyart is a Scots adjective for hair or beards streaked with grey or silver, the sort of dialect word McGonagall might use.

clue.text: Investments being certainty for Trump over successes (7, two words)

indicators.note: in a down entry one piece sitting over another means it comes first

blocks.note: American slang: a lock is a sure thing, and the US president flags the Americanism
ups as in ups and downs, good times

explanation.surface: Political talk of investments that are a dead cert for a president about to triumph again.
explanation.walkthrough: Trump is not a card term here; naming an American president signals that the word for certainty is US slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A lock-up is money tied up in an investment that cannot be quickly realised, so the plural names such holdings.

clue.text: For classicists this hack causes something of a problem

blocks.note: hic is Latin for this
a hack is a dry, harsh cough

explanation.surface: A scholar of the ancient world complains that a jobbing writer is causing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hack' suggests a poor writer, but it is the noise of a cough. Classicists point to Latin. With 1 Across the pair sounds like Billy Cup.
explanation.definitionFit: A hiccough, or hiccup, is used figuratively for a minor setback or glitch, a small temporary snag.

clue.text: Rodent’s whiff mostly on north facing island

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
in a down entry facing north means pointing upward, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: hum is slang for a bad smell
an ait is a small river island

explanation.surface: A rodent's smell hangs over an island seen from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' places the shortened smell above the island word in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The hutia is a guinea-pig-like rodent of the Caribbean islands, such as Cuba and Jamaica.

clue.text: Sure murderer accepting gallows, barely looking up

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece holds another
barely means only just, so the word falls a letter short
in a down entry looking up means the letters run upward

blocks.note: Cain killed his brother Abel in Genesis
the tree is an old word for the gallows

explanation.surface: A killer facing the hangman barely manages to look up from the scaffold.
explanation.walkthrough: The gallows word loses its last letter, turns upward, and sits inside the first murderer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sure and certain are straight synonyms, both meaning confident or beyond doubt.

clue.text: Design eccentricity in jalopy perhaps

indicators.note: one thing set in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: crate is slang for an old, battered car, of which a jalopy is one
e is the mathematical symbol for the eccentricity of a conic

explanation.surface: Someone describes a quirky design feature on an old banger of a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentricity' sounds like oddity, but it is the mathematician's symbol for how far a curve departs from a circle.
explanation.definitionFit: To design something is to devise and bring it into being, which is a verb sense of making.

clue.text: Somehow ruin a synonym for less excellent

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters can come out in any order

blocks.note: taken as written
a word meaning 'a', as in five pounds a head

explanation.surface: A pedant complains that mangling a word ruins a synonym for inferior.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A synonym for' reads like part of the definition, but it asks for a word meaning 'a': PER, as in so much per day.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripe has an old sense of fully developed or excellent, so something more unripe is further from that peak.

clue.text: In an irritating way fish inside frighten on whalers

indicators.note: something inside another is enclosed within it

blocks.note: gally is an old dialect verb meaning to scare, used especially by whalers of startling a whale
the ling is a long fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: Whalers annoyingly scare the fish that are inside their nets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On whalers' is not part of the picture of a ship; it tells you the frighten word belongs to whaling slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Galling means vexing or exasperating, so doing something gallingly is acting in an annoying, chafing manner.

clue.text: What goes inside tight shoe?

definitions.note: the whole clue defines the answer

indicators.note: tight is slang for drunk, and drunken letters stagger out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A riddle about what you wear inside a snug shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tight' seems to describe the shoe's fit, but it means drunk and scrambles the four letters; the whole clue then also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hose are stockings or socks, which are worn on the foot inside footwear.

clue.text: Countermand from Caesar’s unit — anyone with plough

blocks.note: the as was a Roman copper coin and unit of weight
you in the general sense, as in 'you never know'
W is the abbreviation for with
ere is an obsolete verb for to plough, a variant of ear

explanation.surface: A Roman legion's order is cancelled, leaving any soldier with a plough.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a soldier turned farmer, but each word is a separate piece, and 'plough' is an archaic verb rather than the farm tool.
explanation.definitionFit: As you were is the military order revoking a previous command, telling soldiers to return to their former position.

clue.text: One responds when Academy bores head of university college

indicators.note: to bore is to drill into something, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a rector heads some university colleges, such as Exeter College, Oxford
A is the abbreviation for Academy

explanation.surface: Someone reacts when an academic body tediously lectures a college principal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bores' reads as 'tires with dullness', but it means drills into. 'One responds' is the definition, a noun phrase for a thing that reacts.
explanation.definitionFit: A reactor is literally a thing or person that reacts, answering a stimulus with a reaction.

clue.text: Such nobles led by page would be paragons

indicators.note: the answer, once something is put at its head, would become another word; take that front away to get back

blocks.note: a pearl is a paragon, something of the finest quality
P is the abbreviation for page

explanation.surface: Aristocrats with a young attendant at their head would be models of virtue.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: put P in front of the answer and you get a word for paragons. 'Page' looks like a servant boy; it is just the letter P.
explanation.definitionFit: Earls are British peers ranking between viscount and marquess, so they are nobles of a particular sort.

clue.text: Inventor of torture perhaps — namely, one of the Furies

blocks.note: sc. abbreviates scilicet, Latin for namely
the Furies were the avenging spirits of Greek myth

explanation.surface: A torture's inventor is identified as one of the mythical spirits of vengeance.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scavenger's daughter was a Tudor torture device that crushed the body, named after its supposed inventor Sir Leonard Skeffington, whose name was corrupted to Scavenger.
explanation.definitionFit: The man said to have devised the Scavenger's daughter gave his altered name to that torture instrument, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Where sumotori gather round one not moving

indicators.note: people who gather round something enclose it, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: sumo wrestlers live and train in a stable
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Sumo wrestlers crowd around a wrestler who refuses to budge.
explanation.walkthrough: Sumotori is the Japanese word for sumo wrestlers, who belong to training houses called stables.
explanation.definitionFit: Stabile is an adjective meaning fixed or stable, the opposite of mobile, as in a stationary abstract sculpture.

clue.text: Pretence for us in going real

indicators.note: one thing standing for another takes its place, swapping one chunk for another

blocks.note: putting on an act is a pretence
taken as written; these letters are removed
going as in the going rate, the normal one

explanation.surface: A claim that our pretence is turning into reality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' here means 'in place of': the pretence replaces 'us' within a word for normal, as in the going rate. 'Going real' looks like one phrase but splits into wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Actual and real are synonyms, both describing something that genuinely exists rather than being imagined.

clue.text: Kill formality to some extent as a subject for discussion

indicators.note: only to some extent means not entirely, so the word is cut short

blocks.note: top is slang for kill
ice is stiffness or reserve, as in breaking the ice

explanation.surface: A suggestion to drop some ceremony as something worth debating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kill formality' looks like one phrase meaning be informal, but the two words give separate pieces, the second losing its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic is a theme or matter that people talk or write about, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Most reasonable London suburb free of mass nuisance

indicators.note: being free of something means it has been removed

blocks.note: Cheam is a suburb in south London
m is the symbol for mass in physics
a pest is an annoyance

explanation.surface: A suburb is at its most sensible when rid of crowds of irritating people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass nuisance' reads as a crowd problem, but 'mass' is the letter removed and 'nuisance' a separate piece. Cheam is a suburb on London's southern edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Reasonable prices are moderate ones, so the most reasonable option is the least expensive.

clue.text: Drink affected a current recipe first

indicators.note: coming first means standing before the following item in order

blocks.note: camp means theatrically affected or exaggerated
taken as written
R is the abbreviation for recipe, from Latin, used on prescriptions
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: Someone sniffy about cocktails insists on reading the up-to-date recipe before mixing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recipe first' means the R goes before the current's I, reversing the order the words appear in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Campari is a bitter red Italian aperitif, a branded alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Spoil, with mounting woeful wail, wine

indicators.note: mounting means climbing, and in a down entry that makes the letters run upward

blocks.note: to mar is to spoil
alas is a cry of grief

explanation.surface: A spoilt evening of rising lamentation, washed down with wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface lists three things; only the last word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Marsala is a fortified wine from Sicily, named after the port where it is made.

clue.text: Short cleric active on those whipped into line makes good

indicators.note: a short version of a word has letters cut from its end

blocks.note: a reverend is a member of the clergy, often shortened to Rev
A is the abbreviation for active
party whips keep Members of Parliament voting with the party line

explanation.surface: A busy vicar keeps backsliders in order and so reforms them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whipped into line' suggests punishment, but in Parliament whips are party officers who make MPs vote as told.
explanation.definitionFit: To revamp is to renovate or overhaul something, repairing and improving it.

clue.text: I never complain lifting cross then cap

definitions.note: a self-description; the answer is the noun for such a person

indicators.note: lifting raises something, so in a down entry the letters read upward

blocks.note: a rood is a crucifix
a tam is a Scottish bonnet, short for tam-o'-shanter

explanation.surface: A meek person never grumbles while raising a crucifix and then a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: Both the cross and the cap are lifted, each read upward separately. The definition is the whole speaker: someone who never complains.
explanation.definitionFit: A doormat is a submissive person who lets others walk all over them without protest.

clue.text: Flight home for Mitsotakis

blocks.note: first meaning: an old word for a flight of steps
second meaning: the country led by Kyriakos Mitsotakis

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight home' suggests an air journey, but the clue splits after 'Flight'; the archaic word for stairs is spelt like the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Grece is an obsolete term for steps or stairs, and Mitsotakis is the Greek prime minister.

clue.text: English giant shifting grand glut

indicators.note: shifting means moving, and the thousand-pound letter is the one that changes position

blocks.note: Eng is the abbreviation for English
an ogre is a man-eating giant

explanation.surface: An English giant moves away from overindulgence.
explanation.walkthrough: Grand is slang for a thousand, giving G; here it names the letter already in the giant that moves one place along.
explanation.definitionFit: To glut is to fill or gorge to excess, and to engorge is likewise to stuff or swell with too much.

clue.text: Poet’s comparatively dry part of Miserere

indicators.note: a part of something is a piece inside it, so the letters sit within the word

blocks.note: the letters run inside the word

explanation.surface: A poet finds part of a penitential psalm drier than the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: The Miserere is Psalm 51, a plea for mercy. 'Poet's' warns that the answer is a literary word.
explanation.definitionFit: Sere is a poetic adjective for withered or parched, so its comparative means drier.

clue.text: Chinese vase’s plant

blocks.note: Ch is the abbreviation for Chinese
an olla is an earthenware jar or pot

explanation.walkthrough: 'Chinese vase' looks like a single porcelain object, but the two words give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A cholla is a spiny cactus of the south-western United States and Mexico, a type of plant.

clue.text: Good to stay away from Indian vehicle’s nag

indicators.note: something staying away is absent, so a letter is left out

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a gharry is a horse-drawn carriage in India

explanation.surface: A worthy instruction to keep clear of an Indian carriage's old horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nag' looks like the horse pulling the carriage, but it is a verb, to pester.
explanation.definitionFit: To harry is to harass or pester persistently, just as to nag is to badger someone.

clue.text: Scots active independent in leaderless body

indicators.note: without a leader means the front letter is gone
one thing set in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: the flesh is the body as opposed to the spirit
I is the abbreviation for independent

explanation.surface: A Scottish political activist sits as an independent in a body with no head.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Scottish politics, but 'Scots' only marks the definition as a dialect word.
explanation.definitionFit: Leish is a Scots adjective meaning agile, nimble or vigorous, an energetic sense of being lively.

clue.text: Scottish offices being the opposite of schools’ regulator, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the spelling follows the pronunciation

blocks.note: Ofsted, England's schools inspectorate, is said 'off-sted'; swap off for its opposite

explanation.surface: A claim that Scottish administrative buildings work in the reverse way to England's schools inspectorate.
explanation.walkthrough: Ofsted is England's inspector of schools; turning its 'off' into 'on' gives the sound. 'Offices' is the old sense of farm outbuildings, not desks.
explanation.definitionFit: An onstead is a Scottish farmstead, and offices is an older term for a farm's outbuildings and service rooms.

clue.text: Something for drying pipes when night finally falls

indicators.note: the closing letter of the dark hours drops one place lower in this down entry

blocks.note: an oat is a shepherd's pipe made from an oat straw, in poetic use

explanation.surface: Pipes are played as darkness finally comes down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Night finally' is the T, last letter of night; it falls one place downward through the pipes to make the kiln.
explanation.definitionFit: An oast is a kiln used for drying hops, typical of Kent's oast houses.

clue.text: Afternoon spectators on the way somewhere

definitions.note: 'somewhere' marks it as a regional word

blocks.note: A is a dictionary abbreviation for afternoon
the gate is the number of spectators at a match

explanation.surface: A crowd at an afternoon match making their way to the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is not the gemstone but a dialect adverb, which 'somewhere' signals by saying it is used only in some regions.
explanation.definitionFit: Agate is a northern English and Scots adverb meaning astir or under way, going along a road.

clue.text: Cooking pot which divides opinion

blocks.note: first meaning: a large French earthenware or metal stewpot
second meaning: the yeast spread famous for being loved or hated

explanation.walkthrough: The British yeast-extract spread advertised itself with 'love it or hate it', so its name is now used for anything polarising.
explanation.definitionFit: The spread took its name from the French stewpot pictured on its jar, and became slang for divisive things.

clue.text: Description of capers, his exceptionally

indicators.note: something done exceptionally departs from the normal pattern, so the letters break their usual order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An account of a man's antics, which were remarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Description of capers' looks like the definition with its object, but 'of' is the link and 'capers, his' the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecphrasis, or ekphrasis, is a vivid rhetorical description, especially of a work of visual art.

clue.text: Cross about mentor’s disguise

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: cross and testy both mean irritable
rav is a Hebrew title for a rabbi or teacher

explanation.surface: Someone is angry about the costume worn by their teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' could be a crucifix or a verb, but here it is the adjective for bad-tempered; the 's means 'is', linking to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Travesty originally meant dressing in another's clothes, from Italian travestire, so it can mean a disguise.

clue.text: So informally husband getting into shabby schmutter

indicators.note: to get into something is to enter it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: tat is cheap, tasteless clothing or goods; schmutter is Yiddish-derived slang for clothing
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A husband squeezes into some tatty old clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So informally' sounds like a casual aside, but it is the definition: in speech 'that' can mean 'so', as in 'not that bad'.
explanation.definitionFit: Colloquially that works as an adverb meaning to such a degree, as in 'it wasn't that cold'.
